Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00971

Know that a person's inner life in this world will be their outer form in the next. While they live here, the next life is hidden from them. When they move from this world to the next, what was hidden becomes visible to them.
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00972

Calling these outward senses the “gates of Paradise” is a loose way of speaking, not the literal meaning. A house door or city gate opens directly into the place it leads to. Every door should be made of the same kind of thing as the place it opens into. These worldly senses are not like that. The senses that open into Paradise are the senses the soul will have in the next life, and they will remain as long as the soul remains.
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00973

You have learned that the soul itself has hearing, sight, smell, taste, touch, memory, and spiritual hands and feet. It has a seeing eye that looks toward its Lord, an ear that hears God's signs, the words of angels, the birds of Paradise, and the praises spoken by all things. It has a sense of smell for the scent of intimacy and the breezes of holiness; a taste for the foods and fruits of Paradise; and a touch by which it feels the companions of Paradise. These are the soul's inward senses. They and what they sense belong to Paradise, unless something blocks or veils them.
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00974

The senses we use here, however, and the things they perceive, are temporary. They arise and pass away. They can cause painful suffering and a great veil, leading a person to ruin and burning them in the Fire. A soul that follows its desires, gives itself over to lust, and lets Satan rule it becomes a servant of its own appetite. God says, “Have you seen the one who takes his desire as his god? God has let him go astray despite his knowledge, sealed his hearing and heart, and covered his sight.” Each of the seven senses becomes a cause of distance from God and His realm, a gate through which the person serves desire and follows appetite, turns away from the path of guidance and truth, and falls into ruin. “Who can guide them after God? Will you not take heed?” Their state is as God describes: “As for the one who oversteps and prefers the life of this world, Hell will be his home.” This shows that each sense can become one of the seven gates of Hell.
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00975

But if the heart is lit by knowledge and faith, and it moves from possibility to full activity through discipline, worship, and cleansing from the dirt of sin and desire, it becomes like iron purified in fire. Its impurities are removed and it becomes a polished mirror. It then sees the higher spiritual world through each of its senses and finds in it one of the signs of its Lord. Each sense becomes a gate to knowledge of its Lord. Through the particular images it perceives, it draws out universal meanings and understands divine secrets. It reaches the Garden of those brought near and prepares for the highest happiness and nearness to the All-Merciful, in a place of truth before a King of great power.
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00976

The people who follow desire and ignorance, busy with worldly appetites and turning away from the next life and God's signs, persist in arrogance. God says, “He hears God's signs, then persists in arrogance as if he had not heard them.” Their gates are shut and their paths blocked, except for the road to Hell. God says, “We have placed a barrier before them and a barrier behind them, and covered them, so they cannot see.” They have no developed power of understanding that opens the way to divine knowledge and nearness to God. They have no sound heart or listening ear open to the words and warnings of God, so they cannot be saved from the punishment of the next life. Their state there will be just as they admitted when it was too late: “If only we had listened or used our reason, we would not be among the people of the Blaze.” They confess their sin. Away with the people of the Blaze!
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00977

It is now clear that all eight of these senses can become gates to Paradise for those who use them for the purpose God created them. God says, “As for the one who fears standing before his Lord and restrains himself from desire, Paradise will be his home.” The same senses become gates to Hell for those who use them to follow desire and worldly appetites: “As for the one who oversteps and prefers the life of this world, Hell will be his home.”
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00978

You might ask: a house door resembles the house it opens into. Paradise and Hell have completely different natures and kinds of existence. How, then, can the same human senses be the gates of both Paradise and Hell? We answer: the hearing, sight, and other senses of people guided toward happiness differ in their nature from the senses of people ruled by desire and misery. They may share the basic ability to sense, but the senses of the blessed are cleansed of material impurity and lit by knowledge and piety. The senses of the wretched are covered by the darkness of habit and dimmed by ignorance and desire. In short, the blessed person's hearing, sight, and heart have been changed in the next life. They have become suitable gates to Paradise, the home of good deeds and blessings. But the hearing, sight, and heart of the people of Hell have become more wretched, darker, and more impure than they were before. They are now suited to be gates to the home of darkness, ruin, punishment, and pain.
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00979
An unveiling insight
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00980

Know—may God guide you along the straight path to the next life—that Paradise, which those who belong there will reach, is already visible to you today in the place where it is, though not in its outward form. You move through it in your present state without knowing that you are there. Your natural form keeps you from seeing it and the blessings prepared within it: its rooms, trees, rivers, food, and drink. Those with spiritual insight can see what is hidden from others. They can see this place as a green garden, or as Hell, with the toil and strain of its heat and cold, its fires and flames, its snakes and scorpions, its scalding water and Zaqqum.
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00981

People without spiritual insight and clear inner sight remain blind within their veil. They are like a blind person in a garden: the garden is not absent, but they cannot see it. In the same way, most of the people of Paradise are already in Paradise but do not see it. The people of Hell are already in Hell, surrounded by its walls, but do not know it. God points to this when He says, “Hell surrounds the unbelievers,” and, “A Garden as wide as the heavens and earth has been prepared for those who believe.” A sacred report says, “I have prepared for My righteous servants what no eye has seen…” You have learned that a believer's Paradise and an unbeliever's Hell are not things outside their own souls. If they are prepared now, they are already joined to the soul, even if a veil blocks a person from seeing them. God can stand between a person and their own heart—how much more can He stand between a person and the joy or pain within it?
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00982

Some people keep this spiritual sight throughout their lives; others do not. The second group may still be higher in rank, for God has hidden wisdom in His creatures. The people of God have eyes with which they see, ears with which they hear, and hearts with which they understand—but these are not the eyes, ears, and hearts of the body, as you learned earlier. The unbelieving and veiled are deaf, mute, and blind; they do not understand what comes from God and do not return to Him.
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00983
Chapter 27 — Further insight into what Paradise and Hell are
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00984

You have learned that the next life lies between the world of pure intellect and the material world of bodies. Everything there appears in forms that can be sensed and known by a power of the soul that is imagination here and sense there. When a person dies and is freed from this natural body, their small Resurrection begins. They are first gathered into the intermediate world, then into Paradise or Hell at the Great Resurrection.
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00985

The difference between the forms a person sees and takes on in the intermediate world and the forms they see and take on in Paradise or Hell at the Great Resurrection is one of strength and weakness, fullness and incompleteness. Both are particular forms that can be perceived but are not made of matter. In the intermediate world they are seen by imagination; in Paradise they are seen by sense. Yet the sense of the next life is not different from imagination. This is unlike the senses of this world, which are divided among five powers in five different parts of the body. Sight is in the eye, hearing in the ear, taste in the tongue. None can do the work of another: sight cannot hear, hearing cannot see, and neither can smell or taste. The same is true of the other senses. Even sight and touch are not in one place: sight is in the lens of the eye, touch in its outer covering.
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00986

The senses of the next life, however, are all in one place. They do not differ in location or direction, and each can do the work of the others. The relation of forms in the intermediate world to forms at the Great Resurrection is like the relation of a child or unborn baby to an adult.
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00987

Ibn Arabi says in The Meccan Revelations, in chapter 355: “Between the two states of life, death is a time in the intermediate world. There, spirits build intermediate, imagined bodies, just as they built them during sleep. These bodies grow out of our earthly bodies, since imagination is one of their powers.” He continues: “When a person dies, their Resurrection has begun. It is a partial Resurrection. If you understand the Resurrection of one person, you understand the general Resurrection of every person who dies. The time in the intermediate world is to the next life as a woman's pregnancy is to birth. God develops the person there, stage after stage, through different forms of life, until they are born on the Day of Resurrection. This is why we say that when someone dies, their Resurrection begins: the next life starts to appear in the intermediate world, until they are raised from it on the Day of Resurrection, just as a child is born from the womb into the world.”
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00988
“Think about how a person's body develops on earth while they are in the intermediate world. God shapes and adjusts it without following any earlier pattern, preparing it for the next life.”
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00989

In chapter 374 of the same book, Ibn Arabi says: “Know that God has always appeared to hearts in this world, and different thoughts arise because His appearance takes different forms. The different thoughts in a person are themselves a form of God's appearance, though only the people of God know this. They also know that the different forms seen in this world and the next are all different forms of that appearance. He is the One who appears, and He is the inner reality of every thing.
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00990

“In the next life, a person's inner state is fixed, because it is the inner reality of their outward form. The change within them is hidden. It is the new creation that happens in every moment, though people fail to see it. In the next life, what was inward becomes outward. God's appearance is always active there, so a person's outward form changes in the next life just as their inner thoughts change in this life. The forms through which God appears color the person who sees them. This is the divine likeness within imagination. The difference is that in the next life it is outward, while in this life it is inward. The power of imagination stays with a person in the next life.”
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00991

Something like this also happens in this world to some complete people, such as prophets and saints, and to others, such as fortune-tellers, the mentally ill, and people with brain fever. If someone's imagination is strong or their senses are weak, they may see something through imagination as a visible, tangible thing, like the other things they sense. They often confuse it with something in the outer world and wrongly believe that it is physically there.
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00992

Everything a person sees on the Day of Resurrection is seen through imagination. Those forms exist in that world, where they belong. But the things seen through imagination here, such as spiritual ranks, are not treated as lasting realities because they quickly disappear behind a veil. We cannot depend on them here because they soon leave our sight. This world is not where those forms exist. At death, the veil is fully lifted, and the vision of imagination lasts.
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00993

The forms the soul sees are not outside it; they are its own forms. In the next life and in the world of imagination, bodies are spirits and spirits are bodies. This is what it means for meanings and spirits to take bodily form. It happens only in that world. In this world, spirits are connected to bodies but do not take bodily form.
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00994

In chapter 373, Ibn Arabi asks about spirits that appear in the forms of bodies: “Is the spirit itself the form it appears in, without leaving its own spiritual station? Or is that form only in the eye of the person who sees it, as the sky appears blue? Or is the spirit to that form like the soul is to the body—that is, a real image with its own existence, as the soul exists in the body?” Many people overlook this question. They are satisfied with the strange forms they have seen, and their pleasure in the experience keeps them from asking what it was or how it happened.
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00995

“If they could take on spiritual form within themselves, shape their imagined forms by their own power, and make their natural forms yield to them—like a material that receives the forms created by the soul, as jinn take on different shapes—they would understand how spirits take bodily form.”
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00996

“He who knows that an animal's spiritual form passes into the intermediate world when the animal is killed, or that a plant's form passes there when it is cut, will know that it does not vanish. The spirit remains embodied in an imagined form.
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00997
If we see it afterward, we see it as we see any dead creature, human or otherwise.”
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00998

In chapter 381, Ibn Arabi says: “Know that these ranks can be seen only by the eye of imagination, not the eye of the body, even when they appear before us. When God gives them forms, we imagine them and see them as clearly as we see people with our eyes. We see meanings with inner sight. When God makes many things seem few, or few things seem many, we see this through imagination, not bodily sight—even though our bodily eyes are involved in both cases. God says, ‘When you met them, He made them seem few to you, and made you seem few to them,’ and, ‘They saw them twice as many as themselves.’ They did not appear twice as numerous to bodily sight. If they had not seen the many as few through imagination, that would have been false, and the one showing them this would have been lying. But if they saw the many as few through imagination, it was true in that world though not by bodily sight. In the same way, whenever you see something as different from what it is in the outer world, you see it through imagination.”
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00999

“People who have never learned this knowledge cannot understand it. They do not distinguish between kinds of sight. Know that you can reach it only through a power God gives to some of His servants. Consider how, if the Companions had understood this distinction, they would not have said that Gabriel was Dihya al-Kalbi.” “They would have said, ‘This is a spiritual being or a meaning that has taken form; otherwise, we see Dihya with our physical eyes.’ They did not understand the matter fully, though they were honest. When they asked who he was, the Prophet told them that it was Gabriel. Then they understood what they had seen.
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-01000

“Nothing in the world is more easily confused than imagination and bodily sight. If a person is very skilled at this, they may doubt even things they know by direct experience. If they are not skilled, they judge something wrongly and call a form seen in imagination a dark, physical object. If God gives a person a clear power of distinction, they understand the truth.”
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-01001

“Many people of God do not pay attention to this distinction. If a person were always asleep, they would not know that what they see in a dream is imagination. Yet, while awake, they often see things just like the things they see in sleep and do not distinguish between them. Both are real and clearly present in their own way.
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-01002

“This is a wide subject. People who rely on formal learning do not recognize it, nor do philosophers who think they understand wisdom. They have failed to recognize the height of this rank or its value. Only God knows its worth, along with those He chooses from among the prophets and saints. Knowledge of it is one of the first ranks of prophecy.
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-01003

“How beautifully God draws the attention of thoughtful people to it when He says, ‘He forms you in the wombs however He wills.’ Some wombs are in imagination. God forms imagined things in them however He wills, through a spiritual joining and a spiritual pregnancy. He opens the meanings in that womb and gives them whatever forms He wills: Islam takes the form of a camel, the Qur'an of butter and honey, steadfastness in religion of a chain, religion of a loose robe, and knowledge of milk.”
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-01004

In the same chapter, Ibn Arabi also says: “In the world of imagination, God is the place from which a servant's thoughts take form. Every thought the servant has in this world is created by God there, just as God creates the possible things in existence whenever He wills. In this world of imagination, the servant's will follows God's will. The servant wills only what God wills, though in another sense God creates only what the servant wills. Whatever the servant wills in this world may or may not appear to the bodily senses. But in imagination, the servant's will takes effect, as God's will does.
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-01005

“God remains with the servant in this place, creating what the servant wants to create. The same is true of the next life, where the person's inward state becomes outward. Whatever they desire takes form. God acts in response to the person's desires in that world, though not through bodily senses in this one. In this world, God follows the servant's will in this inner realm, and in the next life He follows the servant's desire. But just as the servant's will follows God's will, the servant's desire follows God's desire. God appears in the form through which the servant sees Him, and the servant takes on that form.
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-01006

“We have been given powers of will that act in the world of imagination, and other powers that do not act on the bodily world. This is why things differ—even the divine names differ in rank. A person's active will can affect the will of others, or it may not affect them. For example, ‘You cannot guide whom you love.’” These are the end of his words.
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-01007

All that we have explained and quoted makes this clear: the bodily Paradise consists of forms perceived by the soul's imagination, and desired and enjoyed by it. The soul itself is their only material and source. It is also their maker and the immediate cause that brings them into being. A single human soul, together with all the forms it perceives, is like a great world of the soul, greater than this physical world and all that it contains.
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-01008

All the trees, rivers, buildings, and rooms found there are alive through their own being. Their life is one life: the life of the soul that perceives and creates them. The soul's perception of these forms is the very act that creates them. It does not first perceive them and then create them, or create them and then perceive them. It perceives and creates them together, without one coming before the other.
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-01009

Hell is different. It is not purely spiritual. It is clouded and mixed with this world. It is as if this world, driven by force and control, had been moved into the next life. The person in Hell wants what they cannot get, longs for what harms them, does what they hate, chooses what punishes them, and runs from what would keep them company. They say, as God reports, “If only there were between me and you the distance between east and west! What a terrible companion!”
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-01010

The true nature of Hell and all that is in it is the truth of this world and its desires, appearing to wretched souls as forms that hurt and torment them. These forms burn the body, melt its flesh and fat, change its skin, deform it, and darken its face. All the forms in the next life have their meanings here; “your deeds will return to you.”
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-01011

Since only God is the true maker and cause in the next life, there are no opposing causes, barriers, or forces there as there are here. Whoever agrees with God's judgment and joins their will to God's will, letting their own choice dissolve into His choice, has made their action God's action. Such a person lives in lasting joy and great pleasure. The believer must be like this. I have already explained that the servant's will in Paradise is the same as God's will. The reason is that everything comes from God in the most complete order and the highest good.
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-01012

A person whose heart is sound, whose nature is free of illness, and whose sense of taste has escaped the bitterness of sin accepts God's judgment. They reach the state of being content and of accepting God's will. They want only what God wants; God wants only good, completion, blessing, and joy. Such a person lives in blessing and happiness without end, because they see God's mercy embracing all things. They see in everything the lasting face of Truth, the pure good and absolute beauty that is the source of every good, perfection, and beauty. They rejoice in God and in all things, because everything comes from Him, exists through Him, and returns to Him. They live in a Garden as wide as the heavens and earth. This is why the guardian of Paradise is called Ridwan, “Contentment.” No one enters Paradise or reaches the home of blessing and honor unless they have reached contentment.
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-01013

Those who do not follow the path of knowledge and faith, but remain trapped by worldly desire, have always been prisoners of their appetites and attachments. Desire and appetite oppose wisdom and justice. Since the heavens and earth are established through wisdom and justice, the world of being is spoiled for anyone whose nature opposes its order. Woe to the person whose world has turned against them and whose nature fights the order of existence. The Ruler of the world and the heavens takes vengeance on them because they have become an enemy of God and the world. God says, “If the truth had followed their desires, the heavens and earth and everyone in them would have fallen into ruin.”
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-01014

Such a person is kept from what they desire and what their appetite demands. God says, “A barrier was placed between them and what they desire.” The ignorant person may wish that the stones in their house were pearls, that they would never grow old, and that their body could remain young and beautiful forever. But God's wisdom requires pearls to be rare and valuable, and soil to be plentiful for farming and building. It also requires people to travel toward God, not to spend all their effort maintaining their bodies. Their bodies must grow strong and firm, with dense flesh, so they can bear hardship and resist being harmed.
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-01015

The abode of Hell and punishment is not a separate, independent world or dwelling. It is a mixed state and a dependent form, whose source is this world, carried into the Resurrection by the angels of punishment because of sins, wrong actions, and attachment to worldly things. Understand this carefully. It is a subtle truth, and few mystics have seen the real nature of Hell. Many, however, have seen the true nature of Paradise and what is in it.
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-01016

What supports this view is that Hell is an image of God's anger, just as Paradise is an image of His mercy. We have already shown that God's mercy is essential and reaches all things, while anger is a response. Good things come directly from their source; evil things occur as secondary results. By the same reasoning, Paradise exists in its own right, while the Fire exists as a consequence.
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-01017
A note from a mystic
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-01018

A mystic says about God's words, “Protect yourselves from the Fire whose fuel is people and stones”: Fire can be a remedy for some illnesses. There are illnesses that can be cured only by cauterizing with fire. God says of some people, “They will be branded on their foreheads and sides.” God has made fire a remedy in this case, protecting them from a disease worse than fire itself. What disease is greater than grave sins? God may therefore use Hell as a medicine for them in the next life, just as fire is used to cauterize in this life. By entering Hell, they are cured of something worse: God's anger. For this reason they later leave Hell and enter Paradise, just as worldly laws can protect people from punishment in the next life. These are the mystic's words.
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-01019

This supports what we have said: Hell is not a real, independent home of punishment. It begins when error and disobedience take form in the soul. If Adam's children had not sinned, God would not have created the Fire. Know that the people who suffer are those whose souls were ready for one of the ranks of Paradise, but whose readiness was destroyed by sin. They are like people whose bodies lose the balance and health that suit them. They feel great pain until they return to the balance that was right for them. Or their readiness may be destroyed completely, and their nature may change into one that fits the state that once harmed them. What was illness becomes health, and pain becomes rest.
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-01020

The same is true of those who enter the Fire for a time because of their bad deeds. If the light of faith remains in the heart, the darkness of sin cannot reach its innermost part or surround it completely. Such a person will leave Hell and recover from its punishment. But if disbelief has made the heart completely black, and the darkness of sin has reached its deepest part, that person will never leave the Fire; they will remain there forever. If you want to understand this further, listen carefully to what follows, and keep it from the wicked and base.
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-01021
Chapter 28 — How the people of Hell remain in Hell
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-01022

This is a difficult question, and scholars who rely on formal learning disagree about it. Mystics disagree too. Will the punishment of those who truly belong in Hell last without end? Or will they find happiness in their home of misery, so that their pain ends after a set time? They do agree that unbelievers do not leave Hell and remain there forever. Each of the two homes has its own inhabitants and will be filled.
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-01023

Know that the principles of philosophy show that forced states do not last forever in a thing's nature. Everything in the natural world has an end it reaches in time, and that end is its good and completion. God created things with an inborn power that preserves the good they already have and makes them seek the completion they still lack. As God says, “He gave each thing its form, then guided it.” So every thing loves existence and longs for the fullness of existence. This is its own end, the goal it seeks and moves toward by its nature. The same is true of the ends that lead to it, until we reach the highest end and the greatest good. Something may be held back by an obstacle or forced away from its goal, but such obstacles are not common and do not last forever. We have already explained that if they did, the order of the world would collapse: things would stop working, goodness would disappear, the heavens and earth would fail, and neither this world nor the next would come into being. That is what those who deny the afterlife assume.
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-01024

We can see, then, that all things naturally seek the Real and long to meet Him. Hatred and aversion are passing states. Whoever loves meeting God by nature is loved by God in return. Whoever turns away from meeting Him because of an illness that has come over the soul is turned away from in return. God may punish such a person for a time, until they recover and return to their original nature. Or they may grow used to their painful state. Once they give up hope, their pain and punishment end, and they take on a second nature: the nature of unbelievers who have lost hope in God's special mercy. His general mercy, however, reaches all things. God says, “I send My punishment on whom I will, but My mercy embraces all things.” We also have principles showing that Hell, with its pain and evils, lasts for its inhabitants, just as Paradise, with its joy and good, lasts for its inhabitants. But “lasting” means something different in each case.
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-01025

You also know that the order of this world depends on people with rough natures and hard, unyielding hearts. If everyone were blessed, afraid of God's punishment, and humble before Him, the world would fall apart. No one would remain to build and maintain it. It needs people with hard, defiant natures, such as Pharaohs and impostors; people who do harm, such as human devils, whose cunning and nature fit that role; and ignorant, animal-like people, such as unbelievers. A sacred report says, “I made Adam's disobedience a cause of the world's being built.” God also says, “If We had wished, We could have given every soul its guidance. But My word has come true: I will fill Hell with jinn and people together.” A world made up of only one kind of person would go against wisdom. It would leave all other possible kinds unused, without bringing them from possibility into life. Most levels of this world would then have no inhabitants. The world can function only if it includes low and lesser kinds of things, needed here, with people living in darkness and veiled from the truth. The low and hard-hearted find their pleasures there, far from the home of light, honor, and love.
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-01026

True wisdom therefore requires different levels of readiness, from strong to weak and from clear to clouded. God's unchanging decree has established that both the blessed and the wretched will exist. Since each group exists by God's decree and through the appearance of a divine name, each has its own true end and proper home. When things return to the nature they were made for, they find what suits them and gives them pleasure. But if they are kept away from it for a long time, as God says, “A barrier has been placed between them and what they desire,” they suffer. God appears through all His names and qualities at every level and in every place, as we have explained elsewhere. He is the All-Merciful and the Most Compassionate, but also the Mighty and the Overpowering. A sacred report says, “If you did not sin, God would remove you and bring another people who would sin.”
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-01027

The Arab mystic Ibn Arabi says in The Meccan Revelations: “The people of the two homes enter them: the blessed enter Paradise through God's grace, and the people of Hell enter it through His justice. Their deeds bring them down to those homes, and their intentions keep them there. The pain they suffer as punishment lasts as long as their worldly life spent in unbelief. When that time ends, they find pleasure in the home where they will remain. If they entered Paradise, they would suffer because it does not suit the nature they were given. They take pleasure in the fire and bitter cold, and in the bites of snakes and scorpions, just as the people of Paradise take pleasure in shade and light and in kissing the beautiful companions of Paradise. Their natures call for these things. A dung beetle is harmed by the smell of roses but enjoys filth. Someone overheated is pained by the smell of musk. Pleasure follows what suits a person's nature, and pain follows what does not.” Ibn Arabi also quotes a mystic who says that everyone in Hell will eventually leave for Paradise. Then no one will be left there; its doors will flap in the wind, and watercress will grow at its bottom. God will create new inhabitants to fill it. Qaysari says in his commentary on The Bezels of Wisdom: “Anyone whose eye has been opened by the light of Truth knows that all the world belongs to God. No one has existence, qualities, or power except through Him. Everyone needs His mercy, for He is the All-Merciful, the Most Compassionate. One who has these qualities would not punish anyone forever. Even the punishment that He gives lasts only long enough to bring people to the completion set for them. Gold and silver are heated in fire to remove what clouds them and lowers their quality. So punishment holds kindness within it. As the saying goes: ‘Your torment is sweetness; Your anger, contentment; Your cutting off, connection; Your injustice, justice.’” He ends there. You may ask: do not these views, which say that the punishment of the people of Hell will end, contradict what I said earlier—that their pain will last?
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-01028

I answer: there is no contradiction. The punishment of Hell may never end for Hell as a whole, while the punishment of each person there ends at a certain time. Ibn Arabi says in The Meccan Revelations: “One of the basic states God gave people at their creation is that they worship only Him. They remained true to this nature and to God's oneness. They did not take anything else alongside God and call it God. Rather, they treated other things as gods because they thought these would bring them close to God. That is why God says, ‘Name them.’ Once they name them, it becomes clear that they worship only God, in the place where they say divinity is found. The oneness they affirmed in the covenant is therefore still true, and their original nature remains with them.”
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-01029

I say: this is worship rooted in our nature. We have already said that every natural movement and change in things and souls is toward God, through God, and on God's path. By nature, every person is among those traveling toward Him. By choice and desire, a blessed person draws even closer, moving with greater effort and speed along the path they already follow by nature.
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-01030

But if a person is an incomplete unbeliever, with a heart sealed shut and no power to understand, they are like livestock: they know only animal aims. Their purpose in this life is to guard the world and maintain their bodies. They have no share in the next life. They wander like animals and wild beasts. They are gathered like them, punished like them, judged like them, and given pleasures like theirs. A hypocrite, on the other hand, has turned away from the special nature God gave people and has been shut out from the sky of mercy. Their pain is severe because they have turned away from their own nature and fallen into an abyss through their own actions. Their pain is in proportion to how far they have left that nature and sunk into Hell.
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-01031

Yet mercy is wide. Pain shows that there is an original self within a person that resists their bad animal habits. Conflict between opposing things does not last forever or happen most of the time. It must end either when one side gives way or when the conflict is resolved. But the human soul itself cannot be destroyed. So either the bad qualities disappear when their causes disappear, and the soul returns to its original nature and enters Paradise—unless its bad qualities include beliefs such as worshipping other gods—or else it changes into a second nature and escapes pain and punishment. This is what philosophers mean when they say that the punishment of someone trapped in a false belief may last forever. Someone whose false belief has become firm and deep, along with stubborn ignorance, cannot return to their original nature. They become dead to this life and to the life of reason, though they remain alive in a lower, lesser kind of life. This is what God means when He says of them, “They neither die in it nor live”: they do not die like animals, but they do not live the rational, blessed life either.
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-01032

Ibn Arabi gives these words as evidence that the punishment of those who remain in Hell will end: “Those are the people of the Fire; they will remain in it,” and the Prophet's saying, “No one will remain in the Fire except those who belong there.” Ibn Arabi's reason is that one of the greatest pains a person can suffer is to leave a home they know well. If the people of Hell left it, they would suffer from being far from the place they belong. God made them with a nature suited to that home. I say that this argument is weak. It relies on the words “people” and “belong there,” which can express other kinds of relation, such as being near, being beside something, or having a claim to it.
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-01033

Nor do I agree that leaving a familiar place is the greatest pain, unless we mean the place that fits a person's nature. That claim is hard to prove. A better proof comes from God's words, “We have created many jinn and people for Hell.” If God created someone with the purpose, under His decree, of entering Hell, then entering it must suit their nature and complete their existence. As we said, the end of a thing is its completion. What completes it cannot be painful to it, though it may be painful to someone created for a higher level.
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-01034

Ibn Arabi says in The Meccan Revelations: “The two homes—the home of joy and the home of Hell—are filled. The blessed enter the first through God's grace, and the people of Hell enter the second through God's justice. Their deeds bring them down to these homes; their intentions keep them there. Their pain lasts for a time equal to the length of their worldly life in unbelief. When that time is over, they find pleasure in the home where they will remain, because they would suffer if they entered Paradise, which does not suit their nature. They take pleasure in the fire and bitter cold, and in the bites of snakes and scorpions, just as the people of Paradise enjoy shade and light and the beautiful companions there. Their natures call for these things. A dung beetle is harmed by the scent of roses but enjoys filth; a person with a fever is pained by the scent of musk. Pleasure follows what suits a person's nature, and pain follows what does not.” He also quotes a mystic who says that all the people in Hell will leave for Paradise, until none are left. The gates will then swing in the wind, watercress will grow at the bottom, and God will create new inhabitants to fill it.
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-01035

Qaysari says in his commentary on The Bezels of Wisdom: “Anyone whose eye is opened by the light of Truth knows that the whole world belongs to God. No one has existence, qualities, or power except through Him. All are in need of His mercy, for He is the All-Merciful and Most Compassionate. One with these qualities would not punish anyone forever. Even punishment is only given to bring people to the completion set for them, just as fire melts gold and silver to remove what clouds them and lowers their quality. Punishment therefore holds kindness within it. As the saying goes: ‘Your torment is sweetness; Your anger, contentment; Your cutting off, connection; Your injustice, justice.’”
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-01036

You may say: reason shows that God gains nothing from obedience and loses nothing through disobedience. Everything happens by His decree, and people are compelled even in their choices. How, then, could He make their punishment last forever? The Prophet says that the last to intercede will be the Most Compassionate. Every verse that speaks of their punishment is true, and the words of mystics do not contradict those verses. A thing's being punishment in one respect does not prevent it from being mercy in another. Glory be to the One whose mercy reaches His friends even while He punishes them in this world, and whose punishment reaches His enemies even while His mercy is wide in the next.
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-01037

Ibn Arabi adds: “When the Real appeared to people as they made their covenant with Him, He appeared to them in one of the divine forms. This gave them the courage to worship Him through visible forms. Their original nature remained, because in truth they did not worship those forms. They worshipped them only because they thought those forms would bring them close to God or intercede for them. God reports their words: ‘We worship them only so they may bring us nearer to God,’ and, ‘These are our intercessors with God.’ These two hopes—intercession and seeing God in different forms—are where people will turn in the next life.
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-01038

“When a person understands this divine knowledge, and sees that those people were driven by forces that would eventually lead them back to God, they will pray for them in the darkness and plead for them: ‘Let them enter Your mercy after they have received the punishment they deserve. If they must remain in that home, give them pleasure there, for they too are among all the things Your general mercy embraces.’ It is impossible for God to be limited. He says that His mercy comes before His anger. Anger therefore ends in nothing. If it has any effect, it is still surrounded by mercy.
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-01039

“The prophets say that, on the Day of Resurrection, when they are asked to intercede, God is angry with an anger like no anger before it and unlike any that follows it. This is the most hopeful report to rely on in this matter. That day is when people rise from their graves and stand before the Lord of all worlds. God's anger falls on those who deserve it, and that anger commands them to enter the Fire, suffer, and face punishment—whether they worshipped other gods or committed other wrongs. Some leave through the intercession of those who plead for them; others are brought out by the All-Merciful, as the report says. He then admits them to Paradise, unless they are among the people who truly belong in Hell. The command to enter the Fire therefore applies to all who enter it, both those who belong there and those who do not.
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-01040

“If their punishment lasted forever, God's anger would then be greater than the anger that commanded them to enter Hell. But the prophets say that God will not be angry like that again. Mercy must therefore embrace everyone. It is enough that the Prophet's words say, ‘As for the people of the Fire who belong there’—not simply ‘the people being punished.’ Those who live in Hell need not suffer there. Its inhabitants and keepers include Malik and the other angels, as well as insects, snakes, and other animals brought back to life on the Day of Resurrection. The Fire will not punish them. The same may be true of those who remain there: ‘They neither die in it nor live.’”
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-01041

Scripture gives further proof that God says, “My servants,” to all people. He calls them His own, and He does so only for those already touched by His mercy. So He will not punish them forever, even if they enter Hell. God says: “If the first and last of you, the people and jinn among you, all had the most Godfearing heart, that would add nothing to My kingdom. My servants, if the first and last of you, the people and jinn among you, all had the most wicked heart, that would take nothing away from My kingdom. My servants, if the first and last of you, the people and jinn among you, stood together on one plain and asked Me, and I gave each one what they asked for, that would take nothing from My kingdom.”
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-01042

Everyone naturally dislikes what causes pain and asks God to spare them and give them pleasure. A person may ask with words, or simply through their state—as when a hungry baby cries, even before it understands pain in the body or frustration at being kept from the breast.
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-01043

A person's needs and the states that pass through the heart are beyond counting. I have given you some examples in this chapter. Ibn Arabi ends there. Know that reason and spiritual insight agree on this: the flow of existence, God's creative word and the word “Be,” comes from Him as one undivided whole. It reaches the Footstool, then divides in two. One part flows toward this world of visible things, and the other toward the next world of the unseen. It is like a great river flowing as one, then dividing into two rivers. One runs to the right, the nobler, brighter, and stronger side; the other to the left, the lesser, dimmer, and weaker side. The blessed are people of the right and belong to the next life. The wretched are people of the left and belong to this world. We have already pointed out that the people of this world are the people of Hell, because Hell's true nature and pain grow out of this world and its desires.
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-01044

We have also said that Hell is not a separate home with its own independent existence. There are only two homes: the home of natural bodies that come to be and pass away, and the home of spiritual bodies, alive through their own being and joined to spirits. The difference between this world and Hell is that, while the wretched soul still lives through its natural body, this world is its home of pleasure. It enjoys its desires as animals do. But when it leaves this natural life and enters the next life, its strong attachment to worldly things turns those things into pain. What it once called good now becomes evil. This world's desires become snakes and scorpions in the deepest part of its heart; its food and drink become scalding water and Zaqqum. All these things take forms that match what they mean. The hearts and souls of the people there keep burning with envy, anger, pride, and other traits. Their skin and bodies burn with the fire of nature and desire. The snakes and scorpions formed by their bad habits sting and bite them. This continues as long as God wills.
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-01045
We can now see that there are two homes, and this world and Hell count as one kind of home.
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-01046

With this in mind, we can explain why mystics speak of God's two feet resting on the Footstool. They use this image for the flow of existence from God into this world and the next. They also speak of God's two hands when they mean His qualities of beauty and majesty, or the angels of intellect and soul, because these are channels for His giving and generosity. Their images and ways of speaking agree with scripture and prophetic reports. Ibn Arabi says in chapter 374 of The Meccan Revelations: “The two feet came down to the Footstool, and the spiritual word divided there. The Footstool itself appeared through that word, so the word divided in it. The Footstool is the second form of pure, original bodies after the surrounding Throne. It has two shapes within the universal body, and the two feet came down to it. Each rests in a place. One place is called Hell; the other is called Paradise. There is no other place for the feet to move to. They receive only from their source, the All-Merciful, who is established on the Throne. So they give only mercy.
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-01047

The end returns to the beginning in accordance with wisdom. But there is a road between beginning and end. Without that road there would be no beginning or end. The command that descends must therefore make a journey between them, and a journey can bring hardship and suffering. This is why there is suffering in this world, in the next world, and in the world between them. When the journey ends, the traveler lays down the staff of travel, and finds rest in the lasting home.
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-01048
You may object: “If so, people should find rest as soon as they enter their lasting home, even if it is Hell. Yet that is not what happens.”
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-01049

We reply: “You are right, but you have overlooked something. Travelers are of two kinds. One travels in comfort, served by others, with every desire met, carried in a covered seat, and protected from changes in the weather. This traveler reaches the destination like the people of Paradise. Another walks the road on foot, with little food and few supplies. Even after reaching home, the traveler feels tired and strained for a time, until the hardship passes and rest comes. This is like someone whose home is the Fire. They suffer there, then receive the mercy that reaches all things. Between these two is a third group: they have neither the comfort of the people of Paradise nor the lasting pain of those whose home is Hell. They live between ease and strain. These are the people who leave through the prayers of those who intercede or through the mercy of the Most Compassionate. They have different ranks, depending on how much pain and effort remains for them. It slowly fades in the Fire, and when their time there ends, they leave for Paradise, the home of rest.
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-01050

The last of them are people who did no good, except for their faith and their good manners. Yet God's care had already chosen them for Paradise. The people whose home is Hell remain there. Its doors close and the Fire shuts around them. They give up hope of leaving. Then rest reaches them too, for they no longer fear being taken away, as they did when they saw the mercy of the Most Compassionate bringing people out. God made their nature suited to that home. They would suffer if they left it, as we have explained. When they lose hope, they are glad. This is the first comfort they find there. Once the period of pain has ended, their state is as we described earlier: they find the punishment sweet. It is still called “punishment” because, in the end, it is sweet to the person who experiences it, like scratching an itch. Understand, God willing, the pleasure each home gives its people.
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-01051

Do you not see that the Fire itself remains in pain because it lacks something and is not yet full? It stays that way until the Overpowering One places His foot in it. This is one of the two feet we mentioned on the Footstool. The other rests in Paradise. God says, “Give the believers good news that they have a firm place with their Lord.” The name “Lord” rules over them, and the name “Overpowering” rules over the others, because Hell is a home of power, awe, and majesty, while Paradise is a gentle home of beauty and closeness. The “firm place” is one of the two feet of the Footstool. One is for the Fire and one for Paradise. God cares for both, because both lead to mercy. This does not mean that He does not care, as the ignorant imagine. If He did not care, He would not set punishments for wrongdoing, call Himself angry, or describe Himself as severe in power. These all show His concern for those affected. It is said that Paradise is prepared for the mindful, and a painful punishment for the wretched.
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-01052

Each foot rules over its own home and people. The two feet make people richer or poorer, cause them to live or die, and create pairs of male and female. Without them, there would be no worship of other gods. Each has a home it rules and people it governs. A person who knows God keeps returning to Him and deals with each place as God wants. The ignorant person does not.” Ibn Arabi ends there.
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-01053

Qaysari summarizes: “The three main places in the next life that hold all people are Paradise, Hell, and the Heights between them. Each has a ruling name that draws its own people to it, because they belong to it and fill it. God's promise reaches everyone. In truth, His promise means that He brings each person to the completion meant for them. Paradise is promised to people, but so is Hell. God says, ‘Every soul will come with a driver and a witness.’ As people are drawn to Paradise by the nature that suits it, with the All-Merciful, the Most Compassionate, and the angels of mercy leading them, so people are drawn to Hell by the nature that suits it, with the Mighty, the Overpowering, Satan, and the angels of punishment leading them. Hell itself is promised to them; it was not promised as punishment. The threat of punishment, which comes from the name the Avenger, also reaches everyone in one way, and its effects appear in five groups. The people of Hell include those who worship other gods, unbelievers, hypocrites, and sinful believers. These last include people who know that God is one but do not act on what they know, and those kept from the truth.
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-01054

“When the power of the Avenger rules over them, they suffer in the Fire, as God says, ‘Its walls will surround them.’ After many years and long ages, they grow used to the Fire and forget the joy of God's approval. They say, ‘It is the same whether we grieve or endure; there is no escape for us.’ Then mercy reaches them, and their pain is lifted. For the person who knows God, the punishment is painful in one way, but sweet in another: even while being punished, they see the Real, and that vision is their greatest joy. For those who do not know the true joys, their state is also sweet in one way, because, as a report says, the people of Hell play with the Fire. Playing brings some pleasure, even while they are punished for not having the Garden they believed in—the Garden made of their deeds, with its beautiful companions and palaces.
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-01055

“For people whose nature calls them away from God and toward the Fire, the punishment is painful, though they may actually want it. This is like some unbelievers here who cut their arms and throw themselves from high places. I once saw a man who had driven thick nails through the base of his fingers. He was proud of it, refused to have them removed, and kept them there until he died. For hypocrites, whose nature inclines both to completion and to its opposite, the punishment hurts because they see the completion they cannot reach. But since their pull toward the lesser state is stronger, they accept it. Their pain ends after the Avenger has punished them. Pain becomes pleasure, as when someone first rejects a lowly act, then repeats it until it feels familiar and even takes pride in it.
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-01056

“Those who worship things other than God are punished because they confined the Real to the thing they worshipped and treated the limitless God as if He were limited. Yet, since the thing they worshipped was in truth the Real appearing in that form, they worshipped no one but God, and in this respect God accepts it. Their punishment therefore becomes pleasure for them. Unbelievers suffer greatly, but their nature calls for this state, so they do not feel pain in it. A person may call it punishment when they know there are higher ranks and kinds of joy beyond their own. But punishment does not last forever as punishment: it ends through the help of those who intercede, and at last through the help of the Most Compassionate. This is why watercress will grow at the bottom of Hell, and why the report says, ‘My mercy comes before My anger.’”
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-01057
Chapter 29 — What Hell is made of and what form it takes
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-01058

We have already said that Hell belongs to the same kind of reality as this world. Its source and material are the soul's attachment to worldly things simply because they are worldly. Its form is made up of painful traits, absences, and faults. Absence and defect are negative states, so by themselves they do not act or cause pain. But when the soul experiences them as present, they have a kind of existence for it. In this way they become real evils for the person who has them. Consider the loss of a connection. It is only the absence of a connection that should be there, yet the sense of touch can feel it as intense pain. It is an absence that is experienced and felt. If an absence can be present in this way, it becomes a real evil. The pain of touch is the experience of something that harms the one who feels it.
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-01059

A person's direct awareness of a thing is the thing's actual existence as it appears to them. If what they are directly aware of is an absence, that absence, though still an absence, is present as something real. This is a subtle and difficult point. It also answers a familiar objection: pain is an evil, yet it is an act of awareness, and awareness is something real. This seems to conflict with the philosophers' claim that real evil has no independent being in the world; it is the absence of a thing or of a perfection that belongs to it.
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-01060

It is not enough to answer that pain is evil only as a side effect. Our direct experience tells us that pain itself is evil for the person who feels it, even if we set aside the lost limb, broken connection, or other defect that caused it. Keep this in mind. The form Hell takes in the next life is the soul's experience of pains that come from absences and defects. The wretched soul continues to suffer for as long as it remains in a state where it can recognize those defects and feel the lack of what should be there. The pain ends if either the soul changes into a lower nature, or the defect disappears because the soul's state improves and it turns its attention to higher things it once knew but had been kept from by the distractions of the senses. In either case, the punishment ends.
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-01061

In short, Hell is this world as a worldly state, impressed on the soul as its own condition on the Day of Resurrection. It contains all that is in the heavens and earth in so far as they are flawed and harmful, but not in so far as they are complete and good. In their goodness and completion, they belong to Paradise. While the soul lives here, it sees the things of the world through bodily senses. What those senses show is mixed together: right and wrong, sound and damaged, are hard to tell apart. We see the sun, moon, stars, sky, and earth in a confused way. We assume they last forever and that their light belongs to them by nature, rather than coming from their true sources. We assume the sky and earth really are as our senses show them: fixed, enduring, high or low, and set in a certain order.
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-01062

When the Day of Resurrection comes, these things change. What belongs to them is separated from what does not. What is true is separated from what is false, their borrowed light from their original darkness, and what is good from what is corrupt. God says, “God will not leave the believers as you are until He separates the corrupt from the good.” Hell is the original truth of this world, separated from the good and complete things that do not belong to it. When the Resurrection begins and each group settles in its home, each form returns to its own reality. The people of Paradise are governed by what God gives them in the next life. The people of Hell are governed by what God placed in the matter of this world: in the movements of the heavens and the fixed stars, and in the seven planets whose lights are blotted out. They are still stars, but their light is gone in the Resurrection. The sun is still a sun, but its light is darkened, because its light comes from its original sources and truly belongs to them, not to these physical bodies.
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-01063

Ibn Arabi says in chapter 60 of The Meccan Revelations: “The Fire is close in nature to this world. It is not pure punishment or pure pleasure. That is why God says, ‘They neither die in it nor live.’ The reason is that the divine command placed in the heavens and the movements of the stars remains there, but its effect changes as the forms of the heavens change and the stars lose their light and spread out. Their effects therefore increase or decrease and change in other ways.”
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-01064

He also says: “Know—may God keep us and you safe—that Hell is one of the greatest created things. It is God's prison in the next life. It is called Hell because it is deep. A deep well is called a jahnam. Hell contains burning heat and bitter cold. It has the coldest cold and the greatest heat. From its top to its bottom is a distance of one thousand seven hundred and fifty years. People disagree about whether it was created already or will be created later. They disagree about Paradise too. But for us, the people of spiritual insight and knowledge, both are created and not created. To say that they are created is like saying that someone who builds a house has finished its outer walls. People call it a house, but if they go inside, they see only walls around an open space.”
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-01065

The builder then makes the rooms, halls, shelters, paths, storerooms, and everything the future residents will need. Hell is a home of burning air. Its fire has no embers; its fuel is human beings, stones worshipped as gods, and jinn. God says, “Its fuel is people and stones,” and, “You and what you worship besides God are fuel for Hell.” He also says, “They will be thrown into it—the misguided, their idols, and the armies of Satan.” The tools in Hell come into being through the deeds of the people and jinn who enter it.
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-01066

God made Hell through His quality of anger. The pain and suffering felt by those who enter it also come from that anger. But they exist only when people and jinn enter it. If no one were there, Hell itself would feel no pain, and neither would its angels. Hell and its keepers would be immersed in God's mercy, taking pleasure in praising Him without tiring. God says, “Do not exceed the limits I set, or My anger will fall on you,” and, “Anyone on whom My anger falls has fallen into ruin.” Here, anger itself is pain. Someone who claims to follow our path but does not understand this may say that Hell was created from God's power to compel and that the name “Overpowering” appears there. If that were so, Hell would be busy with itself instead of having power over the tyrants. It could not say, “Is there any more?” or “Some of me has consumed the rest.” God comes to it with the mercy that embraces all things and gives it room to claim more and to rule over the tyrants and deniers. People are mistaken about how Hell was made.
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-01067

One of the strangest reports about this comes from the Prophet. He was sitting with his companions in the mosque when they heard a great crash and became frightened. He asked, “Do you know what that sound was?” They said, “God and His Messenger know best.” He said, “A stone was thrown from the top of Hell seventy years ago. It has just reached the bottom.” Just as he finished speaking, a hypocrite who was seventy years old died in his house. The Prophet said, “God is greatest.” The companions understood that the stone was that hypocrite. From the day God created him, he had been falling into Hell. When he died, he reached its bottom. God says, “The hypocrites will be in the lowest level of the Fire.” God let the companions hear that sound so they would learn. Consider how remarkable the Prophet's words are and how gently he taught them. Ibn Arabi ends there.

A spiritual reminder
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-01069

You have learned that Paradise is above the seventh heaven in rank, but in its true nature it is within the veils of the heavens and earth, because it belongs to the unseen world, which is the inner side of the visible world. You have also learned that the next life grows out of this world. Know, then, that this world is like a kitchen where food for the people of Paradise is prepared. The warmth of the heavens' movements and the rays of the stars ripen it. Human deeds are the material from which the food of their souls and bodies in the next life is made. The more balanced and complete their deeds are, through worldly discipline and bodily effort for God's sake, the better prepared their food, fruit, and drink will be in the next life. It will suit them better and give lasting life greater strength.
Book Eleven — Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-01070

A mystic says: “The heat of the heavens and the rays of the sun and stars are like embers under a cooking pot. They affect the things that grow here and ripen the fruit and minerals, bringing them to maturity. This heat brings benefit, even though it is fire. Whoever understands the next life, the place of Paradise and Hell, and how the fruit of Paradise ripens to give pleasure to its people, will know where the Fire and Paradise are. The fire beneath the bowl-shaped earth of Paradise ripens its fruit. It warms the underside of Paradise's earth, bringing its food into the right state, just as fire under a cooking pot ripens food. The earth of Paradise is musk, according to a report, and musk is warm by nature. The trees of Paradise grow in this musk, just as earthly plants grow in manure, which is warm and makes things rot. This is enough to show the benefit of fire. May God protect us from it in both homes.” The mystic ends there.
